pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–13 years

- **Topic:** Nutrients in a Healthy Diet

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Biology, Nutrition & digestion):** "the content of a healthy human diet: carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water, and why each is needed."

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No direct MS performance expectation on human dietary components; the nearest US content is 5-PS3-1 (energy in food came from the sun) and MS-LS1-7 (food rearranged to release energy / support growth). Diet composition is UK-led. (US/UK divergence.)

- **Operational details:** Children name all seven components of a healthy diet — carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water — give a food source for each, and explain its role (carbohydrates and lipids for energy; protein for growth and repair; vitamins and minerals in small amounts for specific functions; fibre for gut movement; water as the medium for reactions and transport). A key discrimination is which components provide energy (carbohydrates, lipids, and protein in emergencies) and which do not (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water). The move that matters is from 'healthy vs junk food' folk categories to a functional account: each nutrient does a specific JOB, and 'balance' means the right proportions, not eliminating any group.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B. Extends KS2 'animals need the right nutrition and cannot make their own food'; feeds energy calculations, diet-imbalance/deficiency, and digestion. A child is secure when, given a nutrient, they can state a source, its body role, and whether it supplies energy.
bestPractices: Teach each nutrient as a JOB with a food source rather than as a word, and immediately separate energy-providers from non-energy nutrients — the discrimination children most often miss.
Confront folk 'good food/bad food' categories directly: balance means proportion, and no group is simply 'bad'.
Use a real balanced-plate/Eatwell-style model so proportions are concrete and visual.
Address the vitamin/mineral misconception explicitly — needed in small amounts, do specific jobs, carry no energy.
Bridge to the next topics by framing diet quantitatively (energy budget) and diagnostically (what happens if a group is missing).
keyRepresentations: Balanced-plate / Eatwell-guide illustration with the seven nutrient groups
Nutrient → source → role table, colour-coded for energy vs non-energy
Icon key distinguishing energy-providing from non-energy nutrients
Example meals annotated with which nutrients they supply
commonMisconceptions: Believing vitamins and minerals provide energy (they do not).
Thinking all fat is unhealthy and should be eliminated, rather than being a needed energy store.
Assuming protein is only for athletes/muscle-building rather than for all growth and repair.
Treating fibre and water as unimportant because they carry no energy.
Equating 'healthy diet' with eating less, rather than eating the right balance.

learn.summary: Learners (ages 11–13) name the seven components of a healthy diet — carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water — give a food source for each, and state its body role. The central discrimination is which components are the main energy providers (carbohydrates and lipids, with protein a secondary or backup energy source whose main job is growth and repair) versus which provide no or very little energy (vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre, which our own enzymes cannot digest). Activities move learners from 'healthy vs junk food' folk categories to a functional account where each nutrient does a specific job and 'balance' means right proportions, not eliminating any group.

activities.title: Nutrient job cards: source, role, and energy tag
feedback: If a learner tags vitamins or minerals as an energy source: vitamins and minerals are needed only in small amounts to enable specific body reactions (e.g. vitamin C for healthy tissue, vitamin D for bones) and carry no energy; energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and lipids.

If a learner calls protein the main energy nutrient: protein is chiefly for growth and repair; the body uses it for energy mainly when carbohydrates and fats run short or when more protein is eaten than is needed for growth and repair, so it is a backup rather than a main energy source (this misconception may come partly from sports and muscle-building marketing).

If a learner says fat should be cut out completely: lipids are a concentrated energy store, provide insulation and help build cell membranes; harm comes mainly from eating too much, and from some types such as trans fats, not from fat itself.

If a learner dismisses fibre and water: fibre keeps gut contents moving and water is the medium for reactions and transport — both are essential even though neither is a significant energy source for us (water gives none, and fibre cannot be digested by our own enzymes).
activities.rationale: The KS3 curriculum requires naming the seven dietary components and why each is needed, and carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources, while vitamins, minerals and water provide no energy and fibre provides little or none because our own enzymes cannot digest it. Attaching a source, a role and an energy tag to each nutrient directly targets the discrimination learners most often miss. Tap-to-reveal cards, the colour key and lift-the-flap are optional interaction examples that make the energy/non-energy split visible; a non-interactive table or sorting task teaches the same content.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 Biology requires teaching 'the content of a healthy human diet: carbohydrates, lipids (fats and oils), proteins, vitamins, minerals, dietary fibre and water, and why each is needed'.

A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, each with a distinct role; carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources while vitamins, minerals, fibre and water do not provide energy.
learnerActions: For each of the seven nutrients — carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water — write or state one food source, the job it does in the body, and whether it provides energy.

Sort the seven nutrients into two groups: 'main energy providers' (carbohydrates, lipids; protein as a secondary or backup source whose main job is growth and repair) and 'no or very little energy' (vitamins, minerals, water, and fibre, which our own enzymes cannot digest).
Answer two myth-busting prompts explicitly: 'Do vitamins give you energy?' and 'Is all fat bad?', explaining your reasoning in a sentence each.

Optionally use a balanced-plate illustration where tapping a food reveals its nutrient card (e.g. tap chicken → 'protein — building blocks for growth and repair'; tap oil → 'lipid — concentrated energy store and insulation'), with a colour/icon key tagging energy vs non-energy groups and a lift-the-flap reveal for the two myth questions.
activities.intendedInsight: Each nutrient has a distinct job, and only some nutrients supply energy; a healthy diet fills all seven jobs in the right proportions rather than sorting foods into 'good' and 'bad'.

activities.title: Build a balanced plate
feedback: If one nutrient group dominates: flag the imbalance and prompt the learner to add variety so each job is filled in proportion.
If a group is missing entirely: ask which body role is now unfilled and what food could supply it.
Reinforce that a balanced diet means the right proportions, so no whole group is simply 'bad' to include.
activities.rationale: A constructive 'build a balanced plate' task makes proportion concrete and active rather than stated, and bridges toward later quantitative energy-budget work. The live nutrient bars are an optional feedback example that makes the balance mechanism visible; the same task works with a physical plate and a checklist. This goes slightly beyond the naming/role core into evaluation.
sourceClaims: A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, each with a distinct role; carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources while vitamins, minerals, fibre and water do not provide energy.
learnerActions: Assemble a meal by choosing foods for a plate, aiming for the right proportions across the seven nutrient groups rather than maximising any single one.
Watch a live feedback panel (e.g. seven nutrient bars that fill as foods are added) and adjust the meal so no group is overloaded or missing.
Explain in one or two sentences why your finished plate counts as 'balanced' — which groups are present and roughly in what proportion.
activities.intendedInsight: 'Balance' is felt as proportion across all seven jobs, not as eliminating a food group or eating less overall.

activities.title: Food-energy investigation (supervised)
feedback: If a learner predicts a watery food will heat the water most: compare the measured rises — in a fair test with equal masses, the fatty or starchy sample usually produces a much larger rise, showing where food energy is concentrated.
If a learner concludes watery/leafy foods are therefore worthless: point out they still supply vitamins, minerals, fibre and water for non-energy jobs; low energy is not the same as low value.

Emphasise adult supervision, fire-safety and allergy checks (especially nuts) throughout the burning step; results are a comparative demonstration, not a precise calorimetry measurement, because much heat is lost to the surroundings, so compare the two rises fairly using equal food masses, the same water volume and starting temperature, and the same distance.
activities.rationale: This predict–observe–explain investigation gives learners a measured contrast between energy-dense and watery foods, confronting the misconception that all healthy food supplies energy. The probing questions extend the energy/non-energy discrimination to deficiency and the essential role of water.
sourceClaims: A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, each with a distinct role; carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources while vitamins, minerals, fibre and water do not provide energy.
learnerActions: Before testing, PREDICT which of two equal-mass foods will heat water more and why — e.g. a crisp (or a peanut only if no one present has a nut allergy), which is fatty/starchy, versus a grape or lettuce leaf.

Under adult supervision, burn an equal mass of each food at the same distance beneath a boiling tube holding the same volume of water at the same starting temperature, and measure the temperature rise; then repeat with the second food. Very watery foods such as grape or lettuce may barely burn, and that result itself reflects their high water content and low energy per gram.
Compare the measured temperature rises to your predictions and explain what the result shows about where dietary energy sits.

Answer the probing questions: which two of the seven components give most of your energy and which give little or none; if vitamins don't fuel you, why does eating no fruit or veg make a person ill (e.g. scurvy); is any food 'all bad' or does it depend on how much; and why can't you live without water even though it gives zero energy.
activities.intendedInsight: In a fair comparison of equal masses, energy-dense foods (fatty/starchy and low in water) usually release far more measurable heat than watery foods. This challenges the idea that all healthy foods supply lots of energy and locates most dietary energy in carbohydrates and lipids.

activities.title: Check and apply: nutrient roles and energy
feedback: If a learner accepts the 'vitamins for energy' claim: vitamins enable body processes but are not fuel; energy comes from carbohydrates and lipids — sort the foods into 'energy' vs 'other role' to see it.

If a learner is unsure where protein belongs: protein's main job is growth and repair, and it is used for energy mainly when carbohydrates and fats run short or when more is eaten than the body needs for growth and repair, so count it as a backup energy source rather than a main one.
If a learner names the seven components but still mislabels protein or vitamins as the main energy source, or dismisses fibre/water: revisit the specific role of that nutrient before moving on.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorising and responding to a realistic claim are checks that reveal whether a learner can make the energy/non-energy discrimination rather than reciting 'healthy food = energy'. The diagnostic claim mirrors common marketing messages that drive the misconception. Recognition and matching alone do not show the learner can construct the account independently.
sourceClaims: A balanced diet contains carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water, each with a distinct role; carbohydrates and lipids are the main energy sources while vitamins, minerals, fibre and water do not provide energy.
learnerActions: Match each nutrient to its main job (e.g. 'which nutrient is mainly for growth and repair?' → protein).
Categorise each of the seven nutrients as 'provides energy' or 'no energy', treating protein as an energy source only in its backup role.

Respond to a real-world claim, e.g. a cereal box stating flakes are 'packed with vitamins for energy' and a friend saying vitamins give you energy to run around: explain which parts of the diet actually provide energy and what vitamins are really for.
activities.intendedInsight: A secure learner separates the main energy-providers (carbohydrates, fats) from nutrients with other jobs (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water), understands protein as a backup energy source whose main job is growth and repair, and can justify the split against a plausible everyday claim.

constraints: A learner is secure only when, given any nutrient, they can state a source, its body role, and whether it supplies energy — recognition/matching checks alone do not show they can construct this independently.

Treat the tap-to-reveal plate, colour/icon key, lift-the-flap, and live nutrient bars as optional interaction examples, not required mechanisms; the same content can be taught with a table, a paper plate, and sorting cards.
The matching/categorise check assesses the discrimination but does not by itself build it; pair it with the job-card and plate-building tasks.
The food-burning investigation requires adult supervision and fire-safety precautions; measured temperature rises depend on setup and are a comparative demonstration, not a precise calorimetry value.
Address folk categories directly: 'balance' means proportion, protein is for all growth and repair (not only athletes), and no food is simply 'all bad' — it depends on how much.
When categorising nutrients by energy, treat protein as a backup energy source (main job growth and repair) so this stays coherent with how it is framed elsewhere.

An optional 'ask-a-dietitian' conversation wrap may be offered for curiosity questions about specific foods; it is a supplement to the defined-content job-card and plate tasks, not a required or superior medium.
Diet composition here follows UK (DfE KS3) content; there is no direct US NGSS middle-school performance expectation on human dietary components, so framing may need adjustment for other curricula.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original rated a 3D environment as adding 'nothing' and framed a static image as 'the most efficient, high-yield fit'; these categorical catalog-fit preferences have been removed. The neutral underlying observation is retained: nutrient roles are not inherently spatial, so a 3D/spatial environment offers little specific leverage here, though a fixed illustration, interactive, and physical formats each simply offer different experiences without one being universally necessary.

One source (BBC Bitesize) is marked verified:false in the row; the energy/non-energy grouping it supports is widely taught but should be confirmed against the primary curriculum source before relying on it as authoritative.

The claim that protein is used for energy 'only as a backup / in emergencies' is a standard simplification; it holds for typical diets but omits normal ongoing amino-acid turnover. Because the energy/non-energy categorisation is binary, protein is treated as a backup energy source there — flagged so the task does not appear to contradict protein's primary growth/repair role.
Food-burning temperature rises are setup-dependent and comparative only; absolute energy values are not established by this demonstration.

assess.poeTask: Under adult supervision, burn a peanut (or a crisp) beneath a boiling tube of water and measure the temperature rise, then try the same with a grape or a lettuce leaf. Ask students to PREDICT which food heats the water most and why. The fatty/starchy food releasing far more heat challenges 'all healthy food gives energy' and shows where dietary energy really sits.
probeDeeper: Which two of the seven components give you most of your energy, and which give none at all?
If vitamins don't fuel you, why does a person who eats no fruit or veg get ill (e.g. scurvy)?
Is there any such thing as a food that's 'all bad' — or does it depend on how much you eat?
Water gives zero energy — so why can't you live without it?
assess.correctAnswer: Vitamins do not provide energy. Energy comes mainly from carbohydrates and lipids (fats), with protein used only as a backup. Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts for specific body processes (e.g. vitamin C for healthy tissue, vitamin D for bones), and fibre and water provide no energy either.

errorPatterns.pattern: Vitamins give you energy ('take your vitamins for energy')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Vitamins enable body processes but are not fuel; carbohydrates and lipids provide energy. Sort foods into 'energy' vs 'other role'.
errorPatterns.distractor: Vitamins are what give you the energy to run around.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names vitamins as an energy source rather than carbohydrates or fats

errorPatterns.pattern: Protein is the body's main energy food
errorPatterns.nextMove: Protein is chiefly for growth and repair; the body uses it for energy only when carbs and fats run short.
errorPatterns.distractor: Protein is the body's main source of energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls protein the chief energy nutrient (often from sports-drink/muscle marketing)

errorPatterns.pattern: Fat is always bad and has no useful role
errorPatterns.nextMove: Lipids are an energy store, provide insulation and build cell membranes; it is excess, not fat itself, that harms.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says fat should be cut out completely and does nothing good

errorPatterns.pattern: Fibre and water aren't really nutrients / do nothing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Fibre keeps the gut contents moving; water is the medium for reactions and transport. Both are essential without providing energy.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Omits fibre and water, or says they are pointless because they give no energy

responseLevels.gap: Treats all food (or vitamins) as 'energy' and cannot say which nutrients fuel the body versus serve other roles.
responseLevels.full: Distinguishes energy-providing nutrients (carbs, lipids) from those with specific non-energy roles (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water) and gives a food source and a function for each.
responseLevels.partial: Names the seven components and some roles but still calls vitamins or protein the main energy source, or dismisses fibre/water.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A cereal box says its flakes are 'packed with vitamins for energy', and a friend tells you vitamins are what give you the energy to run around. Is that right — which parts of your diet actually provide the energy, and if that's not what vitamins are for, what are they for?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands nutrient roles separates the energy-providers (carbs, fats) from nutrients with other jobs (vitamins, minerals, fibre, water). A child who thinks 'healthy food = energy' or that vitamins are fuel cannot make that split.
